questions.prompt: In Block's (1995) terms, what is access consciousness?

options.text: What an experience is like for its subject
options.why_wrong: That is phenomenal consciousness, the other half of Block's distinction.

options.text: Information available to the rest of the mind for reasoning, report and the control of behaviour
Being awake and responsive rather than asleep or comatose
options.why_wrong: That is creature consciousness, a property of the organism.
That is self-consciousness, a separate notion.

questions.explanation: Access consciousness is a matter of function: content is poised for use in reasoning, report and action. Block's point is that a complete functional story about access may still leave phenomenal consciousness, what the experience is like, unexplained.

sources.citation: Block, N. (1995). On a confusion about a function of consciousness. Behavioral and Brain Sciences 18(2), 227-247.

questions.prompt: Which example shows that creature consciousness and state consciousness come apart?

options.text: A blindsight patient, awake, whose perception guiding her pointing is not conscious
A patient in dreamless sleep who has no conscious states at all
options.why_wrong: Here creature and state consciousness are both absent, so they do not come apart.

options.text: An alert subject consciously seeing a red patch
A person who is conscious of being in pain
options.why_wrong: This illustrates transitive consciousness of a state, not the creature/state split.

questions.explanation: Creature consciousness is a property of an organism (awake and responsive); state consciousness is a property of a particular mental state. An awake creature can have many states that are not conscious, as blindsight shows.

sources.citation: Rosenthal, D. M. (1986). Two concepts of consciousness. Philosophical Studies 49(3), 329-359.
Block, N. (1995). On a confusion about a function of consciousness. Behavioral and Brain Sciences 18(2), 227-247.

questions.prompt: In Rosenthal's terminology, what is the difference between transitive and intransitive consciousness?

options.text: Transitive: a creature is awake; intransitive: one of its states is conscious
options.why_wrong: Wakefulness is creature consciousness, not transitive consciousness.

options.text: Transitive: a state is accessible for report; intransitive: it has a phenomenal feel
Transitive: being conscious of something; intransitive: a mental state's being conscious at all
Transitive: consciousness of the self; intransitive: consciousness of the world
options.why_wrong: Self-consciousness is a separate notion; transitive consciousness can be of anything.

questions.explanation: Transitive consciousness takes an object ('conscious of the noise'); intransitive state consciousness is the property of a state's being conscious. Rosenthal's higher-order theory explains the second in terms of the first: a state is conscious when one is conscious of being in it.

sources.citation: Rosenthal, D. M. (1986). Two concepts of consciousness. Philosophical Studies 49(3), 329-359.
Rosenthal, D. M. (2005). Consciousness and Mind. Oxford: Clarendon Press.

questions.answer_text: The felt, qualitative features of experience: what it is like, for example, to see red or taste coffee.
questions.explanation: Qualia are the currency of the debate over phenomenal consciousness: positions differ on what they are and whether they are physical. Some philosophers, notably Dennett, deny that qualia in the full traditional sense exist.

sources.citation: Jackson, F. (1982). Epiphenomenal qualia. The Philosophical Quarterly 32(127), 127-136.
Dennett, D. C. (1988). Quining qualia. In A. J. Marcel and E. Bisiach (eds.), Consciousness in Contemporary Science. Oxford University Press.

questions.prompt: How did Block (2007) use Sperling's partial-report result?

options.text: As evidence that phenomenal consciousness overflows cognitive access
As evidence that conscious experience is sparse and limited to what can be reported
options.why_wrong: That is the critics' view, which Block opposes.

options.text: As evidence that iconic memory is unconscious
options.why_wrong: Block argues the letters were experienced, not that iconic storage is unconscious.

options.text: As evidence that access and phenomenal consciousness are identical
options.why_wrong: Block uses the result to argue they come apart.

questions.explanation: Observers say they saw all twelve letters, can name only a few, yet can report any cued row; Block reads this as all letters being experienced but only some accessed. Critics reply that observers may experience only a generic impression of letters, with identities reconstructed at the cue, so the overflow is illusory.

sources.citation: Block, N. (2007). Consciousness, accessibility, and the mesh between psychology and neuroscience. Behavioral and Brain Sciences 30(5-6), 481-499.
Sperling, G. (1960). The information available in brief visual presentations. Psychological Monographs: General and Applied 74(11), 1-29.
Kouider, S., de Gardelle, V., Sackur, J. and Dupoux, E. (2010). How rich is consciousness? The partial awareness hypothesis. Trends in Cognitive Sciences 14(7), 301-307.
